name: Quill
workload: Frontend log-call latency for LOG_INFO with int, int, double on 1 and 4 threads, plus 4M-message throughput to file.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 6 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns; 4 threads: 8 ns vs 7047 ns; throughput 6.44M msg/s vs spdlog 2.57M msg/s (derived: about 2.5x)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Formatting is deferred to a backend thread; needs C++17 and fmt; queue-full policy (block, drop or grow) must be chosen.
caveats: Benchmark is run by the Quill author on a tuned, isolated-core system; benchmark code is in odygrd/logger_benchmarks. Latency excludes backend formatting cost.
found_via: GitHub search: C++ low latency logging library faster than spdlog benchmark

name: fmtlog
workload: Frontend latency for static string, integers, doubles and complex format; same messages as NanoLog benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Quill's shootout, 1 thread 3-arg message: fmtlog 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns median; throughput 2.69M vs 2.57M msg/s (about 1.05x, derived). Own README: 6.4 ns vs 156.4 ns (static string).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, Release, -march=x86-64-v3 (Quill shootout); README says GCC 10.2 tested
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4 (README bench: Xeon Gold 6144 @ 3.5 GHz)
tradeoffs: Depends on fmtlib; must call fmtlog::poll() or run a polling thread; log time-ordered via per-thread SPSC queues; Linux focused.
caveats: Throughput advantage over spdlog is marginal (1.05x); the win is front-end latency. Evidence page is Quill's README, not fmtlog's own, whose bench.cc lacks stated flags.
found_via: GitHub search: C++ low latency logging library faster than spdlog benchmark

name: XTR
workload: Frontend log latency (int, int, double message) on 1 and 4 threads in Quill's shootout.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 6 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns; 4 threads: 8 ns vs 7047 ns; throughput 7.73M vs 2.57M msg/s (about 3x, derived)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Linux and FreeBSD x86-64 only; no allocations when logging; consumer thread optional; fmtlib-style formatting.
caveats: Numbers on this page come from Quill's benchmark repo; XTR's own README benchmark (0.9-13 ns on Ryzen 5950X, g++ 15.3.0) has no spdlog column.
found_via: GitHub search: C++ low latency logging library faster than spdlog benchmark

name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
workload: Runtime log-call latency for six message shapes vs spdlog, Log4j2, glog, Boost.Log and ETW; throughput up to 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: README: staticString 7 ns vs spdlog 214 ns median (and glog 1198 ns); complexFormat 8 ns vs spdlog 1776 ns, glog 2569 ns. Quill shootout 1 thread: 8 ns vs 271 ns.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Binary log output must be decompressed offline; Preprocessor version needs a Python build step; C++17 version is a normal library; Linux with POSIX AIO.
caveats: Own README compares old spdlog v1.1.0 and glog v0.3.5 with no stated flags (own numbers are tier C); tier A is from Quill's recent shootout. Output is not human-readable text so throughput is not like-for-like.
found_via: GitHub search: nanosecond logger C++ faster than spdlog asynchronous binary logging

name: MS BinLog
workload: Frontend latency and file throughput in Quill's shootout (binary log output).
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 18 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns; throughput 61.79M msg/s (binary) vs spdlog 2.57M msg/s (derived about 24x, not like-for-like)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Structured binary logs need bread tool to convert to text; coredump recovery; archived read-only repo.
caveats: Repo archived 2026-07-01. Own README gives ns figures and says they are not for direct comparison; no spdlog comparison there. Binary vs text throughput not comparable (Quill notes this).

name: BqLog
workload: 1-10 threads each writing 2M entries (4-param and no-param), time to flush all logs to disk; spdlog in async mode.
claimed_speedup: Compressed mode 6-65x faster than spdlog (async), 7-16x faster than fmtlog, 7-18x than quill, 47-252x than glog; plain text mode also faster. Quill shootout 1-thread latency 125 ns vs spdlog 271 ns (only about 2x).
tradeoffs: Multi-language wrappers (Java, C#, Go, Python); compressed binary format needs decoder; heavier runtime and engine design.
caveats: Own benchmark on Windows only; headline multiples use compressed binary output vs spdlog text. Quill's independent-style table puts BqLog behind fmtlog/XTR/NanoLog on latency. Compiler flags beyond Release not listed.

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Percentile logging latency in microseconds, 1-4 threads, vs spdlog, g3log and reckless.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: guaranteed logger 0 us median (avg 0.35 us) vs spdlog 3 us median (avg 2.59 us), g3log 5 us
hardware: Intel Core i7-2630QM @ 2.00 GHz, Linux Mint 17
tradeoffs: Text logs, C++11, header plus source; guaranteed and non-guaranteed (drop) modes; known-old design.
caveats: No LICENSE file found at repo root (README license not confirmed), so treat as reference. Old compiler and 2016 spdlog; microsecond resolution; flags not stated.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ low latency logging library faster than spdlog benchmark

name: lwlog
workload: picobench of synchronous, buffered, and asynchronous loggers over 8 to 8192 messages.
claimed_speedup: Sync: 12268 vs 1651 ops/s at 8 msgs (7.4x), 2.5x at 8192; sync buffered 319x at 8 msgs; async nonblocking up to 539x in one row
tradeoffs: C++17, compile-time sink config, static buffer for formatting (no allocation per call).
caveats: No compiler, flags or hardware stated; huge ratios (up to 539x) look like different buffering semantics between loggers; not independently reproduced.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ logging library benchmark vs spdlog lwlog

name: haclog
workload: Google Benchmark, 2000 iterations x 5 repeats, write of a struct (u64,u32,i64,i32 and 128-char string) with full pattern, 1 and more threads.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread median 148 ns vs spdlog async 518 ns (3.5x) and spdlog sync 587 ns (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1; build flags not stated (CMake only adds -Wall -Wextra)
hardware: Intel i7-10710U, frequency fixed to 3.2 GHz, Arch Linux
tradeoffs: Plain C API, async, blocking when ring buffer full; efficiency drops under overload.
caveats: Benchmark repo is by haclog's author (first-party); per-run variance high (cv 49% at 1 thread); build type not stated. Same shootout also ranks fmtlog, NanoLog and quill ahead of spdlog.
found_via: WebSearch: C/C++ lock-free logging benchmark: cc_log_benchmark

name: lockfreelog
workload: 5M messages formatted and written to /dev/null, async lock-free SPSC logger vs spdlog async, fmt, printf and iostream.
claimed_speedup: about 28M msg/s vs spdlog async about 5M msg/s (5.3x); about 50M msg/s on Xeon Gold 6348
hardware: Apple M3 (also Intel Xeon Gold 6348 for standalone figure)
tradeoffs: SPSC only; drops messages on a full buffer; consumer spins; C++20 header-only.
caveats: No LICENSE file found, so reference only. Output goes to /dev/null so no I/O cost; single producer vs spdlog async multi-producer queue; spdlog build flags not stated; 3-commit new repo.
found_via: WebSearch: vs spdlog header-only C++20 logger lock-free ring buffer
